body:
Respiration releases energy from food

The nutrients absorbed after digestion provide materials for growth and sources of energy. Cells release usable energy from food molecules through cellular respiration. This energy supports muscle contraction, movement of substances, growth, repair and other activities.

The energy released during respiration is used to make ATP, or adenosine triphosphate. ATP supplies usable energy for many cellular activities and is often called the energy currency of the cell.

Cellular respiration must not be confused with breathing. Breathing is the physical process of moving air into and out of the lungs. Cellular respiration consists of chemical reactions that release energy from food inside cells.

The first stage of glucose breakdown

Glucose begins to break down in the cytoplasm of the cell, forming a simpler substance called pyruvate. The subsequent breakdown of pyruvate depends on the availability of oxygen and the organism or cell involved.

Aerobic respiration

Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to break down food substances and release energy. During the complete aerobic breakdown of glucose, the principal waste products are carbon dioxide and water. The oxygen-dependent stages of this process occur mainly in the mitochondria.

In simplified form, glucose + oxygen produce carbon dioxide + water + usable energy.

Aerobic respiration makes substantially more usable energy available from the same amount of glucose than the anaerobic pathways described below. It is the main energy-releasing pathway in most human cells under ordinary conditions.

Anaerobic respiration

Anaerobic respiration, in the school-level comparison, refers to the release of energy from food without using oxygen. It releases less usable energy from a given amount of glucose than complete aerobic respiration.

In yeast, glucose can be broken down without oxygen to form ethanol, carbon dioxide and energy. This process is called alcoholic fermentation.

When skeletal muscle cells cannot obtain enough oxygen to meet an intense, short-term energy demand, they can produce lactic acid through an anaerobic pathway while obtaining energy from glucose.

Comparing the pathways

FeatureAerobic respirationAnaerobic pathways
OxygenRequiredNot required
Energy obtained from glucoseGreaterLess
Important locationCytoplasm followed by mitochondriaCytoplasm
Typical productsCarbon dioxide and waterEthanol and carbon dioxide in yeast; lactic acid in muscle cells

Formation of lactic acid during intense activity is associated with limited oxygen availability in the school-level explanation. However, muscle cramps can have several causes; they should not all be attributed solely to lactic acid accumulation.

Do plants also carry out respiration?

Yes. Plants require ATP for cellular activities just as animals do. Their living cells respire during the day and night. Photosynthesis produces and stores organic food using light energy, whereas respiration releases usable energy from that food. These processes have different purposes and can occur in the same plant.

Prelims focus

  • Cellular respiration releases energy from food and supports ATP formation.
  • Glucose first breaks down into pyruvate in the cytoplasm.
  • Oxygen-dependent breakdown occurs mainly in mitochondria.
  • Aerobic respiration produces carbon dioxide and water and releases more usable energy.
  • Yeast can produce ethanol and carbon dioxide anaerobically; muscle cells can form lactic acid.
  • Trap: Breathing is not the same process as cellular respiration.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 5, “Life Processes”, Section 5.3, pp. 87–89, 2026–27 reprint; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 10, “Respiration in Organisms”, pp. 108–110 and 116–117, 2018–19 printing.]

title: Cellular Respiration: Aerobic and Anaerobic Energy Release

body:
How air reaches the lungs

Humans obtain oxygen from atmospheric air through the respiratory system. Air normally enters through the nostrils, passes through the nasal cavity and then travels towards the lungs through the respiratory passage, including the trachea, or windpipe.

The nasal passages contain hairs and mucus that help trap dust and other particles. The trachea is supported by cartilaginous rings that help prevent the airway from collapsing.

The trachea divides into 2 main bronchi, each entering a lung. Inside the lungs, the passages branch into smaller bronchioles that lead to numerous tiny air sacs called alveoli.

Inhalation and exhalation

Inhalation is the movement of air into the lungs. During normal inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and moves downwards, while the ribs move upwards and outwards. These changes increase the volume of the chest cavity, lowering air pressure inside the lungs relative to the atmosphere and allowing air to enter.

Exhalation is the movement of air out of the lungs. During normal quiet exhalation, the diaphragm relaxes and moves upwards, while the rib cage returns towards its resting position. Chest cavity volume decreases and air flows out.

Why are alveoli suitable for gaseous exchange?

Alveoli are tiny air sacs with very thin, moist walls. They are surrounded by networks of blood capillaries. Their enormous combined surface area and short diffusion distance allow gases to move efficiently between air and blood.

Oxygen moves from alveolar air into the blood because of a difference in oxygen concentration and partial pressure. Carbon dioxide moves from the blood into the alveolar air, from which it is removed during exhalation.

Oxygen entering the blood binds mainly to haemoglobin, the respiratory pigment in red blood cells. Carbon dioxide is transported from tissues to the lungs largely in dissolved chemical forms carried by the blood.

Why does breathing become faster during exercise?

When muscle activity increases, cells require more usable energy. The body generally responds by increasing both the rate and depth of breathing and by increasing blood circulation. These changes help deliver more oxygen and remove additional carbon dioxide.

One breath consists of 1 inhalation followed by 1 exhalation. The breathing rate is the number of complete breaths taken in 1 minute. It varies with activity, age, health and other conditions.

Breathing and cellular respiration are linked but distinct

Breathing moves air. Alveoli exchange gases between air and blood. Blood transports these gases. Cellular respiration uses oxygen inside cells to release energy from food. Each stage is necessary for efficient aerobic energy production in a large animal such as a human.

Prelims focus

  • Air passes through the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to reach alveoli.
  • Alveoli have thin walls and a rich capillary network for gas exchange.
  • During inhalation, the diaphragm moves downwards and the chest cavity expands.
  • During exhalation, the diaphragm returns upwards and chest cavity volume decreases.
  • Haemoglobin in red blood cells transports most oxygen in the blood.
  • Trap: Oxygen is exchanged in the lungs but is used for aerobic respiration inside cells.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 5, “Life Processes”, Section 5.3, pp. 88–90, 2026–27 reprint; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 10, “Respiration in Organisms”, pp. 110–115, 2018–19 printing.]

pictures.caption: The opposite movements of the ribs and diaphragm during breathing.

title: Human Breathing, Alveoli and Exchange of Respiratory Gases

body:
Blood is a transport tissue

The human body requires a continuous supply of nutrients and oxygen and a means of removing wastes. Blood carries these substances through a network of vessels. Blood is classified as a fluid connective tissue.

It consists of a liquid portion called plasma and suspended components that include red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

Components of blood

ComponentMain function
PlasmaTransports dissolved nutrients, hormones, salts and many waste substances
Red blood cellsCarry oxygen mainly through haemoglobin
White blood cellsHelp defend the body against infections
PlateletsHelp blood clot and reduce blood loss after injury

Haemoglobin is an iron-containing pigment that gives red blood cells their characteristic colour and allows them to transport oxygen efficiently. A deficiency of haemoglobin can reduce the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood.

Blood clotting helps prevent excessive blood loss when a vessel is damaged. Platelets participate in the clotting process, although they are not the only substances involved.

The 3 main types of blood vessels

Blood vessels form a continuous network connecting the heart to body tissues and back again. The main categories are arteries, veins and capillaries.

FeatureArteriesVeinsCapillaries
Direction of blood flowAway from the heartTowards the heartBetween small arteries and small veins
WallsThick, muscular and elasticGenerally thinnerExtremely thin, usually 1 cell thick
Blood pressureRelatively highRelatively lowLower than in supplying arteries
Special featureWithstand pressure from heartMany contain valves preventing backflowPermit exchange with surrounding tissues

Why are capillaries essential?

Large arteries branch into progressively smaller vessels, eventually forming capillary networks within organs. Capillary walls are thin enough for oxygen, nutrients and other substances to pass between blood and surrounding tissue fluid. Carbon dioxide and many dissolved wastes move from tissues towards the blood.

Capillaries then connect to small veins that return blood towards the heart. Without this fine network, blood in large vessels could not directly supply every individual body cell.

Arteries and veins are defined by direction, not oxygen content

Most arteries in the systemic circulation carry oxygen-rich blood, and most systemic veins carry oxygen-poor blood. However, this is not the correct way to define the vessels.

The pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood away from the heart to the lungs. The pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood towards the heart from the lungs. These are important exceptions to the usual association between vessel type and oxygen content.

Lymph as a supporting transport fluid

Some fluid leaves blood capillaries and enters spaces around cells. The lymphatic system collects excess tissue fluid and eventually returns it to the bloodstream. Lymph also transports much of the fat absorbed from the small intestine.

Prelims focus

  • Plasma is the liquid component of blood.
  • Red blood cells contain haemoglobin; white blood cells defend against infection.
  • Platelets help blood clot.
  • Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry blood towards it.
  • Capillaries have very thin walls suitable for material exchange.
  • Trap: The pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood, while pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 5, “Life Processes”, Section 5.4.1, pp. 91–94, 2026–27 reprint; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 11, “Transportation in Animals and Plants”, pp. 121–125, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 6, “Tissues”, pp. 73–75, 2018–19 printing.]

pictures.alt: A small artery feeds thin-walled capillaries, where oxygen and nutrients leave blood and tissue wastes enter it, before blood flows into a small vein.
pictures.caption: Capillaries connect circulation with the needs of individual body cells.

title: Blood, Arteries, Veins and Capillaries

body:
The heart is a muscular pump

The heart is a muscular organ located in the chest cavity, slightly towards the left. Its continuous rhythmic contractions maintain the circulation of blood. The heart is divided into 4 chambers: 2 upper atria and 2 lower ventricles.

The right and left halves are separated by a partition called the septum. This separation helps prevent oxygen-rich blood from mixing with oxygen-poor blood. Valves maintain one-way flow through the heart by preventing significant backward movement of blood.

Functions of the 4 chambers

ChamberReceives blood fromSends blood towards
Right atriumBody through the venae cavaeRight ventricle
Right ventricleRight atriumLungs through pulmonary artery
Left atriumLungs through pulmonary veinsLeft ventricle
Left ventricleLeft atriumBody through aorta

The ventricles have thicker muscular walls than the atria because they pump blood out of the heart. The left ventricle has particularly thick walls because it must pump blood throughout the body, whereas the right ventricle pumps blood only to the lungs.

Tracing the circulation of blood

Oxygen-poor blood returning from the body enters the right atrium through the venae cavae. It passes into the right ventricle and is pumped through the pulmonary artery to the lungs. At the lungs, blood releases carbon dioxide and takes up oxygen.

Oxygen-rich blood then returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. It enters the left ventricle, which pumps it through the aorta into arteries supplying the body. After exchanging substances in tissue capillaries, the blood returns through veins to the right atrium.

What is double circulation?

Double circulation means that blood passes through the heart twice during one complete journey through the body's circulation.

  • Pulmonary circulation: Blood travels from the right side of the heart to the lungs and returns to the left side.
  • Systemic circulation: Blood travels from the left side of the heart to the body tissues and returns to the right side.

This arrangement helps maintain efficient oxygen delivery and keeps the oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood streams largely separate in a healthy human heart.

Heartbeat and pulse

A heartbeat involves rhythmic contraction and relaxation of the heart muscle. The pressure wave produced as the heart pumps blood can be felt in certain arteries as the pulse. In a normal rhythm, each heartbeat generally produces a corresponding arterial pulse.

Heart sounds can be heard using a stethoscope. Heart rate and pulse rate generally increase during physical activity because the tissues need increased blood flow.

Prelims focus

  • The human heart has 4 chambers: 2 atria and 2 ventricles.
  • The right side receives oxygen-poor blood; the left side receives oxygen-rich blood.
  • The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs through the pulmonary artery.
  • The left ventricle pumps blood to the body through the aorta.
  • Double circulation includes pulmonary and systemic circulation.
  • Trap: Pulmonary veins return blood from the lungs to the left atrium, not to the right atrium.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 5, “Life Processes”, Section 5.4.1, pp. 91–93, 2026–27 reprint; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 11, “Transportation in Animals and Plants”, pp. 123–126, 2018–19 printing.]
